food.text: Kashk is a range of dried dairy products made from strained yogurt, drained buttermilk or sour milk. Charles Perry points to a 13th century Arabic cookbook, Wasf al-Atimah al-Mutadah, which says dried yogurt was a Turkomen-style kashk. Kashk is used in Persian cooking to this day.

According to Encyclopædia Iranica, the earliest known mention of pilaf, in any of its spellings, is in the 14th-century Persian satirical poem Mūš-o gorba by Ubayd Zakani. The rice dish that later spread widely appears in Persian verse well before any recipe called it pilaf.

Sharbat is a sweet cordial made from fruit or flower petals and usually served chilled. It is believed to have originated in Iran. In the 11th century, the Persian scholar Ibn Sīnā listed several syrups in his Canon of Medicine.

The English word saffron comes from the 12th-century Old French safran, which traces back to the Persian zafarān. That name is said to come from the older zarparān, meaning 'gold-strung', for the flower's golden filaments or the rich golden hue the spice gives to food.

Rose water likely originated in Persia, where it is called golāb, from gul (rose) and ab (water). Before the technique for making it was developed, rose petals were used in Persian cuisine to perfume and flavour dishes. Medieval Arab and Persian chemists later refined the distillation process.

In the 12th century, the Persian book Zakhireye Khwarazmshahi described different types of sharbat in Iran. Its author, Gorgani, named Ghoore, Anar and Sekanjebin among them, showing that these cooling drinks were already a varied tradition.

art.text: From the 13th century to the early 16th century, Iran and Central Asia were ruled by two dynasties descended from Genghis Khan: the Ilkhanate (1256-1353) and the Timurids (1370-1506). This period saw the construction of some of the largest and most ambitious Iranian monuments of the Islamic world.
The Seljuqs seized Baghdad in 1048. During their time the center of culture, politics and art production shifted from Damascus and Baghdad to Merv, Nishapur, Rayy and Isfahan, all in Iran.

Timurid architecture attained the height of sophistication in the first half of the 15th century, under the patronage of Gawhar Shad, wife of Shah Rukh (r. 1405-1447). Her monuments were mainly found in Mashhad and Herat.

Textiles of Iran and Iraq in the 14th century incorporated Chinese phoenix designs in silk and gold thread, which came through the Mongol realm from the Yuan Dynasty. Italian weavers adopted these designs from the second half of the 14th century.
art.source_title: Mongol elements in Western medieval art

art.text: Gawhar Shad's mausoleum and mosque complex (1417-1438) has been destroyed or severely damaged since the 19th century. Some of the surviving vaulting and decoration inside her mausoleum still hints at its original quality.

The Seljuks introduced mausoleums with a square or polygonal floor plan, which later became a common form of monumental tombs. Early examples are the two octagonal Kharraqan Towers (1068 and 1093) near Qazvin and the Mausoleum of Sanjar (c. 1152) in Merv, which has a square base.

Muslim Spanish paper arrived early in Iran, in the 13th century, and coloured papers were used often. Page margins were decorated by inserting a different paper, a tradition that appeared in the 15th century, or by sprinkling them with gold, following a Chinese custom.
Seljuq palace centres in Iran often featured stucco figures. This was part of the art production that shifted to Iranian cities such as Rayy and Isfahan under the Seljuqs.

war.text: The Mongol invasion of Iran began in 1219. During 1220 and 1221, Bukhara, Samarkand, Herat, Tus and Nishapur were razed and their populations slaughtered. In 1221 Genghis Khan destroyed the city of Gurganj, and most if not all of the ancient Iranic Khwarazmian people were killed or pushed out. The invaders leveled cities, burned libraries and destroyed qanat irrigation systems in north-eastern Iran, leaving many abandoned towns.

The Ghaznavid ruler Mahmud began an invasion of India in 1000, but the dynasty could not hold power for long, particularly after Mahmud died in 1030. By 1040, the Seljuqs had taken over the Ghaznavid lands in Iran.
In 1025, Mahmud of Ghazni used 400 elephants against Ali-Tegin. War elephants were a major part of Ghaznavid armies in Khorasan during this era, meant to charge, break ranks and spread terror.

The Mongol invasion of Iran began in 1219 after two diplomatic missions sent by Genghis Khan to Khwarezm had been massacred. The Khwarezm-Shah fled the invaders and died on an island off the Caspian coast.
At the battle of Dandanqan in 1040, the heavy Ghaznavid war elephants proved to be a disadvantage. The Ghaznavids were bested by the greater mobility of the Seljuks.
In 1008, elephants were used against the Kara-Khanid invasion of Khorasan. This is perhaps the only recorded instance of war elephants being used in deep snow.
At the Battle of Ghazni in 1117, 50 Ghaznavid elephants at first scared off the Seljuk cavalry. Then the Seljuks managed to wound the lead elephant, which caused the rout of the whole Ghaznavid army.

During the invasion of Transoxiana in 1219, Genghis Khan used a Chinese specialist catapult unit alongside the main Mongol force, and used it again in 1220. The Chinese may have used the catapults to hurl gunpowder bombs, since they already had them by this time.
The Seljuks also adopted war elephants. At the battle of Saveh in late 1118, 18 of them proved pivotal for Ahmed Sanjar's victory.

literature.text: Ferdowsi, who lived from 935 to 1020, wrote the Shahnama, the Book of Kings. The work resulted in a revival of Iranian culture and the expansion of the Iranian cultural sphere.

The ruba'i, a rhymed four-line poem or quatrain, has been continually popular in Iran since the medieval period. Omar Khayyam and Mahsati Ganjavi of Seljuk Persia are among the famous poets who wrote poetry only in this format.
Rumi, one of the best-loved Persian poets, was born in Balkh or Wakhsh but lived in Konya, then the capital of the Seljuks in Anatolia. He wrote in Persian there.

Around the 5th century, priests at the Sassanid court began compiling a huge chronicle called the Khwaday Namag, or Book of Kings. The Middle Persian original is lost. Its contents survive through Arabic translations and in the Shahnameh by Firdausi, a verse version in New Persian finished around 1000 AD.

Omar Khayyam (1048–1123) is often recognized as a scientist in his native Persia. His Rubaiyat was freely translated, or paraphrased, by Edward FitzGerald in 1859. That version made his verses among the most quoted Persian poetry in English.

The Ghaznavids conquered large territories in Central and South Asia and adopted Persian as their court language. As a result, Persian literature came to be produced well beyond Iran itself, including in places such as Afghanistan, Pakistan and India.

Nizami Ganjavi's Khamsa, or Five Treasures, opens with Makhzan-ol-Asrâr, influenced by Sanai's Garden of Truth. The other four poems are medieval romances, including Layla and Majnun, which derived from Arabic sources. Nizami reworked his source material in a substantial way.

Jahan Malek Khatun was an Injuid princess and poet, and a contemporary of Hafez. Injuid princesses usually wrote under a pen name that disguised their identity and emphasised their piety, but she did neither. Contemporary poets used the concept of Jahan, "the World", for an imaginary female figure who was ruthless and seductive, conspiring to murder her many lovers. Using that name neither concealed her feminine identity nor emphasised religious virtue, which made it notable.

Azerbaijani literature in Iran has a tradition originating from the 13th-century Mongol conquest of Iran. It incorporates both Turkic and Iranian influences. Many poets from Azerbaijan wrote both in Azerbaijani and in Persian.

Most Zoroastrian Middle Persian texts, including the Zend commentaries, date from the 9th to the 11th century, long after Middle Persian had stopped being spoken. The surviving manuscripts are usually 14th-century copies, so the texts reflect living Middle Persian only indirectly.

The earliest known illustrated Khamsa of Nizami is a Jalayirid manuscript created in Baghdad in 1386-88. Another lavish copy was made in Tabriz in 1481, commissioned by the Aq Qoyunlu ruler Yaqub Beg. Such manuscripts were painted with miniatures for courts.

Like many 14th-century ghazal writers, Jahan Malek Khatun was overshadowed by her famous contemporary Hafez. Her work was published in Iran for the first time only in 1995. Sheema Kalbasi introduced it to Western audiences with an English translation in 2007.
Under the Timurids, Turkic poetry prospered, based on the vernacular known as Chaghatai. Today this language is called Uzbek and Uyghur. It is of Turkic Qarluq origin.

Jahan Malek Khatun's parents married in 1324, so she was born after that date. Her father was Jalāl al-Dīn Masūʿdshāh, who was deposed in 1339 and fled to Luristan, where Yagi Basti's men killed him while he was bathing in 1342. As an only child she received the attention usually given to sons, and her education was exceptionally good even by Injuid noble standards. Her uncle Abu Ishāq brought her up and guarded her until he fell from power in 1353, and Mubariz al-Din Muhammad, who captured Shiraz, executed him in 1357.

science.text: Khayyam, who lived from 1048 to 1131, is described as one of the greatest polymaths of all time. He presented a theory of heliocentricity to his peers. His contributions to laying the foundations of algebra are also noteworthy.

Windmills of Persian origin were panemones, made of six to 12 sails covered in reed matting or cloth. They were used to grind grain or draw up water. They were widely used across the Middle East and Central Asia, and by the 11th century the vertical-axle windmill had reached parts of Southern Europe.
Al-Biruni (973–1048) measured the radius of the Earth using a new method. It involved observing the height of a mountain at Nandana, now in Pakistan.
science.source_title: Science in the medieval Islamic world

science.text: Al-Biruni and Avicenna, among others, described the preparation of hundreds of drugs made from medicinal plants and chemical compounds. Islamic doctors also described diseases like smallpox and measles, and challenged classical Greek medical theory.
science.source_title: Science in the medieval Islamic world

science.text: Around 1390, Mansur ibn Ilyas wrote Tashrih al-badan (Anatomy of the body) in the Persian language. The work contained comprehensive diagrams of the body's structural, nervous and circulatory systems.

In July 1017, after the murder of the Khwarazmshah Abu'l-Abbas Ma'mun, Mahmud of Ghazni invaded Khwarazm and took Kath. Al-Biruni and most other scholars left with the victorious Mahmud, possibly as prisoners, and were brought to Ghazni. From 1017 he served as court astrologer and accompanied Mahmud's campaigns in the Indian subcontinent, at a time when, as the article puts it, Hindus had suffered waves of destructive attacks on many of their cities and Islamic armies had taken numerous Hindu slaves to Persia. The resulting Tārīkh al-Hind, finished around 1030, is the work on which his reputation as an Indologist chiefly rests.

In 998 al-Biruni went to the court of the Ziyarid amir of Tabaristan, Qabus. There he wrote al-Āthār al-bāqiya ʿan al-qurūn al-khāliya, "The Remaining Signs of Past Centuries", on historical and scientific chronology, probably around 1000, though he later revised it.
tags: The Remaining Signs of Past Centuries

science.text: The Mas'udi Canon was an encyclopaedia of astronomy, geography and engineering. Al-Biruni dedicated it to Mas'ud, son of the Ghaznavid sultan Mahmud of Ghazni.

Several Chinese astronomers worked at the Maragheh observatory, which Nasir al-Din al-Tusi founded in 1259 under the patronage of Hulagu Khan in Persia. One of them was Fu Mengchi, also called Fu Mezhai.
The court of the Ma'munids at Gurganj was gaining a reputation as a gathering place for brilliant scientists. There al-Biruni collaborated again with his former teacher Abu Nasr Mansur.

Some experimental studies in recent years have evaluated medieval Iranian medical remedies using modern scientific methods. These studies raised the possibility of reviving traditional treatments on the basis of evidence-based medicine.

politics.text: The Seljuk Empire was founded in 1037 by Tughril and his brother Chaghri, who co-ruled its territories. It spanned about 3.9 million square kilometres, from Anatolia and the Levant to the Hindu Kush, and lasted from 1037 to 1308.
Timur established the Timurid Empire in 1370 and ruled it until his death in 1405. He saw himself as the great restorer of the Mongol Empire of Genghis Khan and regarded himself as his heir.

The Ilkhanate was a Mongol khanate founded in the southwestern part of the Mongol Empire. It was established after Hülegü, a grandson of Genghis Khan, inherited the West Asian and Central Asian lands when his brother Möngke Khan died in 1259. Its realm was officially known as the Land of Iran.

The Khwarazmian Empire began as vassals of the Seljuks and the Qara Khitai. Under Ala ad-Din Atsiz, who ruled from 1127 to 1156, Khwarazm became independent from its neighbors. It eventually became the most powerful state in and around Persia, defeating the Seljuk and Ghurid empires.

Ghazan Khan (r. 1295-1304) began as a leader of the traditional nomadic Ilkhanid Mongols but converted to Islam. He aided a cultural and economic resurgence in which urban Iranian culture was of primary importance.

After defeating Masud I at the Battle of Dandanaqan in 1040, the Seljuks set up a Persian bureaucracy to administer their new state, employing Khorasanians. Tughril served as its nominal overlord. By 1046, the caliph Al-Qa'im had sent Tughril a diploma recognising Seljuk rule over Khorasan.

Muhammad II of Khwarazm ordered a contingent of merchants sent by the Mongols to be killed, and Genghis Khan declared war on the Anushtegin dynasty in 1219. The Mongols overran the empire and occupied its major cities and population centers between 1219 and 1221. Iran was ravaged by the Mongol detachment under Jebe and Subutai, who left the area in ruin.

Ilkhanid rulers, beginning with Ghazan in 1295, converted to Islam. In the 1330s outbreaks of the Black Death ravaged the Ilkhanate, and both Abu Sa'id and his sons were killed by the plague by 1335. The realm then broke apart into a succession of short-lived khans.

Tughril Beg entered Baghdad in 1055 after expelling the Shiite Buyid dynasty, and was the first Seljuk ruler to style himself Sultan and Protector of the Abbasid Caliphate. From then on the Abbasids were only puppets in Seljuk hands. In 1058 the caliph granted Tughril the title "King of East and West".

In 1029, Majd al-Dawla was facing an uprising by his Daylami troops in Ray and asked Mahmud of Ghazna for help. Sultan Mahmud arrived, deposed him, and replaced him with a Ghaznavid governor. This ended the Buyid dynasty in Ray.

Ulugh Beg, a famed patron of science who was himself an astronomer and mathematician, was executed in 1449 after a revolt by his son Abdal-Latif Mirza. His death plunged the Timurid Empire into civil war. Abu Sa'id Mirza later briefly reunited most of it.

Under Abu Sa'id, the non-Mongol emirs Sharaf-ud-Din Mahmud-Shah and Ghiyas-ud-Din Muhammad were given unprecedented military authority, which irked the Mongol emirs. After Abu Sa'id died in 1335, Ghiyas-ud-Din put Arpa Ke'un, a descendant of Ariq Böke, on the throne. This triggered a succession of short-lived khans.

Abu Sa'id Mirza was defeated and executed in 1469 by Uzun Hasan, bey of the Aq Qoyunlu, and the Timurid possessions were permanently divided. Husayn Bayqara ruled in Herat from 1469 to 1506 and proved to be the last of the great Timurids.

philosophy.text: Ibn Sina, known in the West as Avicenna, lived from about 980 to 1037 and was a preeminent philosopher and physician of the Muslim world. He served in the courts of various Iranian rulers. His philosophy belonged to the Peripatetic school derived from Aristotelianism, and he is considered among its greatest proponents.

Under the Seljuq ruler Malik Shah (1072–1092), Iran enjoyed a cultural and scientific renaissance, largely attributed to his brilliant Iranian vizier, Nizam al Mulk. The Seljuq leaders also built religious schools in all the major towns.

Avicenna began writing The Book of Healing in 1014, completed it around 1020, and published it in 1027. It is his major work on science and philosophy, intended to "cure" or "heal" ignorance of the soul. Despite its title, it is not concerned with medicine.

Avicenna, born near Bukhara, successfully reconciled Aristotelianism and Neoplatonism with Kalam. Because of this, Avicennism eventually became the leading school of Islamic philosophy by the 12th century.
The Seljuq rulers brought Abu Hamid Ghazali, one of the greatest Islamic theologians, and other eminent scholars to their capital at Baghdad. They encouraged and supported the scholars' work.

Sunni Islam ruled Iran from the Ghaznavids through the Mongol invasion and the Ilkhanate, which kept Shia Islam out of power. That changed in 1310, when the Mongol ruler Ghazan converted to Shia Islam.

Avicenna wrote most of his philosophical and scientific works in Arabic but also wrote several key works in Persian. Of the 450 works he is believed to have written, around 240 have survived, including 150 on philosophy and 40 on medicine.

Al-Ghazali (1058–1111) argued that the term Qiyas refers to analogical reasoning in a real sense and to categorical syllogism in a metaphorical sense. Ibn Hazm (994–1064) disagreed with some scholars of the time, holding instead that Qiyas means categorical syllogism in a real sense.

After Avicenna was forced to become vizier by Shams al-Dawla, he sometimes clashed with Shams al-Dawla's troops. He remained vizier until Shams al-Dawla died of colic in 1021. He declined to stay on under the successor Sama' al-Dawla and went into hiding with his patron Abu Ghalib al-Attar, where he was secretly in contact with Ala al-Dawla Muhammad, the Kakuyid ruler of Isfahan. The Buyid court suspected him of this correspondence, had Attar's house ransacked and imprisoned him in the fortress of Fardajan for four months.

In 1012 Avicenna travelled through Khurasani cities toward Gorgan, hoping to visit the Ziyarid ruler Qabus, a cultivated patron whose court attracted distinguished poets and scholars. When he arrived he found that Qabus had been dead since the winter of 1013. Avicenna then left Gorgan for Dihistan but returned after becoming ill. There he met Abu 'Ubayd al-Juzjani, who became his pupil and companion.

culture.text: Islamization in Iran was a long process. The Muslim population rose from approximately 40% in the mid-9th century to close to 90% by the end of the 11th century. Historian Seyyed Hossein Nasr suggests the Persian nationality of the rulers helped speed up conversion.

Before the devastating Mongol conquest of 1219 to 1221, Sunni Islam was the predominant form of Islam in Iran. That changed with the advent of the Safavid Empire, which ruled from 1501 to 1736. After Ismail I captured Tabriz in 1501, he proclaimed Twelver Shia Islam the state religion and ordered the Sunnis to convert. Because most of his subjects were Sunni, he enforced it violently and put to death those who opposed him; thousands were killed in the purges that followed, and in some cases entire towns were eliminated for refusing to convert.

The Ghaznavids, who ruled from 989 to 1149, founded an empire that became the most powerful in the east since the Abbasid Caliphs at their peak. Their capital at Ghazni became second only to Baghdad in cultural elegance. It attracted many scholars and artists of the Islamic world.

The Il-Khans in the thirteenth century and the Timurids in the fifteenth century deliberately patronized Persianate high culture. Under their rule new styles of architecture developed, Persian literature was encouraged, and miniature painting and book production flourished. Their broad peace made travel safe, so scholars, artists and fine books circulated freely.
Ghazan, a Mongol ruler, converted to Shia Islam in 1310. Until then the Mongol Ilkhanate, established after the invasion, had kept Shia Islam out of power. Sunni Islam had ruled since the Ghaznavids.

The Mongol invasions stimulated Persianate culture, because many people had to seek refuge in a few safe havens, primarily India. There scholars, poets, musicians and fine artisans intermingled and cross-fertilized. The invaders under Genghis Khan and Timur thus helped concentrate specialists of high culture.
Yarsanism is believed to have been founded in the late 14th century. Its faith rests on belief in one God, who manifests in 1 primary form and 6 secondary ones. Together they are the Holy Seven.

The Nizari Ismailis, a secret sect, established their base in Iran, and Hassan-i Sabbah captured the fortress of Alamut in 1090. They controlled the area around it for more than 150 years and sporadically sent out adherents to strengthen their rule by murdering important officials. Several theories on the etymology of the word "assassin" derive from these killers. The Nizaris used the fortress until a Mongol raid in 1256.

The Buyid dynasty emerged in Daylaman, in north central Iran, about 930. It extended its rule over central and western Iran and into Iraq until 1048. The Buyids were Zaidiyyah Shia, so Shia rule persisted in Iran before Sunni Ghaznavid power spread.
